explanation:
## The program

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
{
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; ++j)
    {
        if (j > 1) std::cout << ' ';
        std::cout << i * j;
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

## How many times does the inner body run?

`n` times for each of `n` passes of the outer loop, so `n * n` in
all. The inner loop is re-entered from scratch every time: `j` is
declared in its header, so it comes back into existence at 1 on each
pass, and there is nothing to reset by hand.

That is the main reason to declare the counter in the header rather
than above the loop. With `int j;` outside, the inner loop would
leave `j` at `n + 1` and the second row would print nothing until
somebody remembered to set it back.

## Where the newline goes

```
inside the inner loop    one number per line
between the two loops    one row per line        ← what is wanted
after both loops         the whole table on one line
```

Three placements, three different programs, no compiler error
between them. When a nested loop prints the wrong *shape*, this is
almost always what it is.

## Separator before, not after

```cpp
if (j > 1) std::cout << ' ';
std::cout << i * j;
```

The alternative — print the number, then a space, then strip the
last one — means either building the line in a string first or
testing `j < n` instead, which works and reads as "all but the last"
rather than "all but the first". Both are fine. What does not work
is printing the space unconditionally and hoping nobody notices: a
trailing space is a different line to a comparison that is checking
exact output, and it is invisible on screen.

This is the most common reason a solution that looks right fails
here. If a case fails and the output looks identical, pipe it
through something that shows the ends of lines.

## What this does not check

Alignment. A real multiplication table would pad the columns so they
line up, which needs `std::setw` from `<iomanip>` and a decision
about how wide. The exact-match grading here wants single spaces, so
the exercise deliberately asks for the simpler thing; the
constraint that `n <= 12` is what keeps that from looking silly.
